beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Reading the output won't tell me whether the agent is safe, so I need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a reading list and I didn't open it

beats.trigger: Apply named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain)
beats.got: The module covers five named risk patterns. I know injection already, but supply chain for skills is a fresh angle.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I should have a list of checks before this goes near real people.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: nothing new, I see the tool-call loop daily. The framing as a boundary is neat but I got it in two seconds.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: Fair question. I haven't bet mine on any of my agents, honestly.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: nothing new, I know this from running engineering.

beats.trigger: The attack surface is the instruction set.
beats.got: Prompt injection through a document the agent reads is an attack on its decisions, not on code. That matters for letting non-engineers connect it to Confluence and mail.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: There are five mitigation shapes with names. I already use scope and review, and I'll steal the split one.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: Writing down the residual risk and accepting it on record is the process. It's a bit ceremonial for my taste, but a CTO needs the paper trail.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: I always add access and context. Taking it away to shrink the damage is a move I haven't made.

beats.trigger: Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it.
beats.got: My plan to plug it into everything for the sales team is the opposite of this. Annoying, and probably right.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a recap with some mood music.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: nothing new, I already write skills. This one is a security skill.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The raw run splits policy rules into ones a file can check and ones that need a human. I haven't seen that split before.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript
beats.got: I told the agent which data is touchy at our company instead of reading the policies myself. That's faster, and I liked it.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: The agent interviewed me for a while and then wrote the two-lens skill. I answered quickly and skipped some questions.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: I can hand questions back to the agent with a one-liner. I'll use that.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: nothing new, saving a skill is routine for me.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The policy files are source material and the skill is the reusable judgment. Fine.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The goal is running the loop, not getting a pass.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new, a slash-command check I do daily.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit flagged a few things I thought were fine and left some as I-can't-tell. That cost me a few minutes of reading the report, but the report was useful.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The ranked risk report showed injection paths I would not have found on my own, mostly through documents my agents read.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: I applied one mitigation and wrote down what's left. I'd have kept going, but stopping at one is probably right.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: When stuck on a risk, take the evidence to legal or security. I know that, so nothing new.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: My weekend builds are prototypes by this definition. That stings a bit.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The skill carries over to the next agent and the report carries the decisions.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the audit session and adds one to five rules to the root instructions file for future sessions.
beats.got: The agent writes rules into the instructions file from this session. Good, but I'd normally do this on the fly.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: A skill can be handed to a teammate, but that doesn't solve who owns and maintains it. That's my sales-team blocker exactly.

beats.trigger: Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a recap of the four points.

beats.trigger: Write one sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: I have homework before module 5. Probably I won't do it.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: nothing new, more pre-reading.

take_homes: Prompt injection works by getting the agent to decide something harmful through text in a document it reads. That changes what I let non-engineers connect it to.
Take access away before adding it. Scope, split, filter, gate and review are the five mitigations, and I'll use split and scope first.
Keep a reusable audit skill with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, and run it against each new agent I build.

monday.move: Run the agent-audit skill on the sales-team setup before I build more of it, and cut one connection (probably the mailbox) from it.
monday.who: me, then the security lead if the report has an I-can't-tell I can't close
monday.when: Monday morning, or maybe later in the week if I get pulled into something
monday.stop_condition: One mitigation applied and the residual written down
monday.blocker: Nobody in sales asked for it and nobody owns maintaining it. A skill doesn't fix that.

misconception.why: 'Same prompt, same files, same tools, different session, different answer' and 'One passing test is one sample' undercut my habit of treating good-looking output as good. Output also can't show whether a document steered the agent. I still skipped steps in the exercises, so I'm not fully changed.

one_line: Most of it I knew, but the give-it-less part and the injection-through-documents part were new, and the audit skill is worth keeping.
